ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the Board for Ethical Questions in Science of the University of Innsbruck (reference number 03/2021).
Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal.
More movement instructions were expected to increase working memory load because participants had to maintain the action imagery longer and compare more details with the position judgement image.
Participants were recruited from the experimenters' acquaintances and undergraduate Psychology students at the University of Innsbruck, who received course credits.

Another 14 participants were excluded due to insufficient data quality, as defined by the following criteria, of which several applied to the same participants: needing more than three attempts on at least two of four comprehension checks, providing inconsistent responses (e.g., on the The final sample (76 female, 40 male, 3 diverse) was on average 25 years old (SD = 7.2; range = 19-63).
Most participants were right-handed (112 right, seven left).
All participants were native German speakers, reported having no hearing impairments, and normal or corrected to normal vision.
Informed consent was obtained at the beginning of both sessions.
For half of the trials, one body part that participants had been instructed to 326 imagine moving was depicted in the wrong direction (non-matching; see Fig. 1A).
table.formatted: For half of the trials, one body part that participants had been instructed to 326 imagine moving was depicted in the wrong direction (non-matching; see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>).

table.text: Following FPJT instructions and a comprehension check, participants completed four practice trials (two movements), with feedback on correctness and response time.
In this task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of auditorily presented digits ranging from 1 to 9.
After a two-digit practice trial with feedback on whether the correct digits were recalled in the correct order, participants completed a test block consisting of 16 trials (no feedback).
In the Corsi Task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of illuminated squares.
In each trial, participants were presented with ten blue squares on a black background, with their locations varying across trials.
After the FPJT baseline condition, participants completed the Digit Span Task and the Mental Body Rotation Task.
Participants completed either Session A or Session B first and completed the other session after an interval of 7-14 days.

Such a rehearsal strategy is plausible because the movement instructions likely engaged the motor system (Dupont et al., 2023), and participants were asked to use (and also reported) internal visual and kinesthetic action imagery.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We targeted a minimum sample size of N = 100 to provide sufficient power (> 80%) to detect the interaction between FPJT condition and Digit Span Task performance in a generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) on FPJT trial errors (further including number of movements and the interaction between FPJT condition and Corsi Task performance; see Supplementary Material for details).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 100, alpha_level = NA_real_, power = 0.8, effect_size = NA_real_, effect_size_metric = NA_character_, software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "We targeted a minimum sample size of N = 100 to provide sufficient power (> 80%) to detect the interaction between FPJT condition and Digit Span Task performance in a generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) on FPJT trial errors (further including number of movements and the interaction between FPJT condition and Corsi Task performance; see Supplementary Material for details)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted #### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethical approval was obtained from the Board for Ethical Questions in Science of the University of Innsbruck (reference number 03/2021).
live_data_statements: Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal.
More movement instructions were expected to increase working memory load because participants had to maintain the action imagery longer and compare more details with the position judgement image.
Participants were recruited from the experimenters' acquaintances and undergraduate Psychology students at the University of Innsbruck, who received course credits.

Another 14 participants were excluded due to insufficient data quality, as defined by the following criteria, of which several applied to the same participants: needing more than three attempts on at least two of four comprehension checks, providing inconsistent responses (e.g., on the The final sample (76 female, 40 male, 3 diverse) was on average 25 years old (SD = 7.2; range = 19-63).
Most participants were right-handed (112 right, seven left).
All participants were native German speakers, reported having no hearing impairments, and normal or corrected to normal vision.
Informed consent was obtained at the beginning of both sessions.
For half of the trials, one body part that participants had been instructed to 326 imagine moving was depicted in the wrong direction (non-matching; see Fig. 1A).
Following FPJT instructions and a comprehension check, participants completed four practice trials (two movements), with feedback on correctness and response time.
In this task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of auditorily presented digits ranging from 1 to 9.
After a two-digit practice trial with feedback on whether the correct digits were recalled in the correct order, participants completed a test block consisting of 16 trials (no feedback).
In the Corsi Task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of illuminated squares.
In each trial, participants were presented with ten blue squares on a black background, with their locations varying across trials.
After the FPJT baseline condition, participants completed the Digit Span Task and the Mental Body Rotation Task.
Participants completed either Session A or Session B first and completed the other session after an interval of 7-14 days.

533 An exploratory analysis revealed that participants were significantly slower to identify 534 a correct (baseline: M±SD = 2.67±0.90 s; articulatory suppression: M±SD = 2.52±0.93 s) than 535 an incorrect position judgement image (baseline: M±SD = 2.26±0.77 s; articulatory 536 suppression: M±SD = 2.13±0.77 s) in both conditions (baseline: t(118) = 6.90, p < .001, mean 537 difference = 0.41 s, 95% CI [0.29, 0.53], d = 0.63; articulatory suppression: t(118) = 7.35, p < 538 .001, mean difference = 0.39 s, 95% CI [0.28, 0.49], d = 0.67).

Participants completed an adapted FPJT under baseline and articulatory suppression conditions, with articulatory suppression serving as a selective interference manipulation targeting verbal rehearsal.

Such a rehearsal strategy is plausible because the movement instructions likely engaged the motor system (Dupont et al., 2023), and participants were asked to use (and also reported) internal visual and kinesthetic action imagery.
Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:7, File = c("data-anaylsis.R", "OpenSesame-local/data-prep.R", 
"OpenSesame-online/data-prep.R", "PsychoPy-local/data-prep.R", 
"PsychoPy-online/data-prep.R", "plots.R", "power-analysis.R"), 
    "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
    "—"), Basis = c("none", "none", "none", "none", "none", 
    "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `data.rdata` to `data/data.rdata` (in OpenSesame-local/data-prep.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 2 ran without error, 4 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("data-anaylsis.R", "OpenSesame-local/data-prep.R", 
"OpenSesame-online/data-prep.R", "PsychoPy-local/data-prep.R", 
"PsychoPy-online/data-prep.R", "plots.R", "power-analysis.R"), 
    Outcome = c("errored", "errored", "ran_ok", "errored", "errored", 
    "ran_ok", "timed_out"), Detail = c("undefined_variable", 
    "runtime", "", "runtime", "runtime", "", "timeout"), "Time (s)" = c(23.1, 
    1.2, 1.4, 1.2, 0.9, 9.3, 300.3)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "data-anaylsis.R", "Missing variable" = "overdisp_fun", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("OpenSesame-local/data-prep.R", "PsychoPy-local/data-prep.R", 
"PsychoPy-online/data-prep.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L, 
1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", "data", "data")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

1 call to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. text.text: When imagining actions based on verbal movement instructions, maintaining an evolving mental representation across successive instructions is important.

We examined this process from a working memory perspective, asking whether maintenance of verbally instructed action imagery depends on verbal working memory or can be sustained by action imageryrelated processes.
In an adapted Final Position Judgment Task (FPJT), participants imagined three to six successive movements from listening to standardized movement instructions.
They then judged whether an image of a human figure matched their imagined final position.
Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal.
This articulatory suppression increased errors but performance remained above chance, suggesting that performance was not reducible to verbal rehearsal.
Converging with this, FPJT errors were associated with visuospatial, but not verbal, working memory, with these associations not varying by FPJT condition.

Articulatory suppression reduced reported verbal rehearsal and action imagery quality, whereas in both conditions, more than 80% reported visual rehearsal of instructed body parts to maintain imagery.
Visual rehearsal was associated with fewer errors in baseline.

Our results suggest that maintaining verbally instructed action imagery in the FPJT relies on action imageryrelated visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal playing a supporting role.
Given that FPJT performance also covaried with mental body rotation and mental paper folding performance, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.
The mental simulation of actions without physical execution (action imagery; Decety et al., 1989; Jeannerod, 1994) has attracted sustained scientific interest across disciplines and research areas.
text.formatted: The mental simulation of actions without physical execution (action imagery; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Decety et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Jeannerod, 1994)</ref> has attracted sustained scientific interest across disciplines and research areas.

text.text: Fundamental research investigates the cognitive processes (Moran & O'Shea, 2020) and neural mechanisms (Hardwick et al., 2018) involved in action imagery, as well as its overlap with executed actions in physiological markers (Decety et al., 1991; Guillot et al., 2010) and temporal properties (Guillot et al., 2012; Guillot & Collet, 2005).
text.formatted: Fundamental research investigates the cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Moran & O'Shea, 2020)</ref> and neural mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Hardwick et al., 2018)</ref> involved in action imagery, as well as its overlap with executed actions in physiological markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Decety et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Guillot et al., 2010)</ref> and temporal properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Guillot et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Guillot & Collet, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These lines of work enhance our understanding of the contribution of action imagery to motor learning (Dahm et al., 2025) and its overlap with movement planning during action execution (Glover & Baran, 2017; Jeannerod, 2001).
text.formatted: These lines of work enhance our understanding of the contribution of action imagery to motor learning <ref type="bibr">(Dahm et al., 2025)</ref> and its overlap with movement planning during action execution <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Glover & Baran, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Jeannerod, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Applied research aims to translate related insights into practice by using action imagery to support motor rehabilitation and enhance athletes' performance (Holmes & Collins, 2001; López et al., 2019; Simonsmeier et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Applied research aims to translate related insights into practice by using action imagery to support motor rehabilitation and enhance athletes' performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Holmes & Collins, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">López et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Simonsmeier et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, clarifying the mechanisms involved in action imagery is imperative for both theoretical and practical advances.
Accumulating evidence indicates that action imagery draws on executive functions (Glover et al., 2020) and overlaps neurally with working memory (Van Caenegem et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Accumulating evidence indicates that action imagery draws on executive functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Glover et al., 2020)</ref> and overlaps neurally with working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Van Caenegem et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: On a behavioral level, working memory was shown to mediate age-related differences in action imagery ability (Schott, 2012) and to be associated with outcomes of action imagery practice (Malouin et al., 2004).
text.formatted: On a behavioral level, working memory was shown to mediate age-related differences in action imagery ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Schott, 2012)</ref> and to be associated with outcomes of action imagery practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Malouin et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: These findings may reflect both general cognitive demands and the role of working memory in maintaining and manipulating mental action representations.

Action imagery (also referred to as movement imagery, motor imagery or action simulation; Moreno-Verdú et al., 2024) involves four processes (Cumming & Eaves, 2018; Kosslyn et al., 1995; Kraeutner et al., 2020): generation (creating a mental action representation), maintenance (keeping it active over time), manipulation (transforming or updating it), and inspection (evaluating its content).
text.formatted: Action imagery (also referred to as movement imagery, motor imagery or action simulation; <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Moreno-Verdú et al., 2024)</ref> involves four processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Cumming & Eaves, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Kosslyn et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Kraeutner et al., 2020)</ref>: generation (creating a mental action representation), maintenance (keeping it active over time), manipulation (transforming or updating it), and inspection (evaluating its content).

text.text: For example, imagining tossing and striking a volleyball involves generating an action representation of oneself, the volleyball and the environment.
This action representation needs to be maintained and manipulated as the imagined action goes on.
Ultimately, imagery inspection will determine whether the volleyball landed at the intended location.
These processes situate action imagery within the framework of working memory, which provides the mental workspace for maintaining and manipulating information (E. K. Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These processes situate action imagery within the framework of working memory, which provides the mental workspace for maintaining and manipulating information (E. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Working memory can be conceptualized as comprising multiple components (Baddeley et al., 2020; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974).
text.formatted: Working memory can be conceptualized as comprising multiple components <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Baddeley et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Baddeley & Hitch, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: These components are the central executive that allocates attention and resources, the phonological loop that maintains and manipulates verbal and auditory information (which we refer to as verbal working memory), the visuospatial sketchpad that maintains and manipulates visual and spatial information (which we refer to as visuospatial working memory), and the episodic buffer that integrates information across these components and long-term memory (for an alternative working memory conception, see Gade et al., 2014; Oberauer, 2009).
text.formatted: These components are the central executive that allocates attention and resources, the phonological loop that maintains and manipulates verbal and auditory information (which we refer to as verbal working memory), the visuospatial sketchpad that maintains and manipulates visual and spatial information (which we refer to as visuospatial working memory), and the episodic buffer that integrates information across these components and long-term memory (for an alternative working memory conception, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Gade et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Oberauer, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Working memory has been proposed to support the formation of mental models for action planning (Baddeley, 1993), and action imagery has been described as the internal rehearsal of motor acts within working memory (Decety & Grèzes, 1999).
text.formatted: Working memory has been proposed to support the formation of mental models for action planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Baddeley, 1993)</ref>, and action imagery has been described as the internal rehearsal of motor acts within working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Decety & Grèzes, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, research on imagery and working memory has developed into two largely separate literature streams (Tong, 2013).
text.formatted: Yet, research on imagery and working memory has developed into two largely separate literature streams <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Tong, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This lack of literature integration is apparent for action imagery, whose functional relationship with working memory remains insufficiently understood (Moran & O'Shea, 2020) and sparsely considered in theoretical accounts (Hurst & Boe, 2022).
text.formatted: This lack of literature integration is apparent for action imagery, whose functional relationship with working memory remains insufficiently understood <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Moran & O'Shea, 2020)</ref> and sparsely considered in theoretical accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Hurst & Boe, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, clarifying how the verbal and visuospatial components of working memory are involved in maintaining action imagery is an important step towards integrating working memory and action imagery research.

Although action imagery can incorporate multiple sensory modalities, visual and kinesthetic imagery are typically emphasized (Krüger et al., 2022), with their relative contributions varying across task demands and individuals (Krüger et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although action imagery can incorporate multiple sensory modalities, visual and kinesthetic imagery are typically emphasized <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Krüger et al., 2022)</ref>, with their relative contributions varying across task demands and individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Krüger et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Combining visual and kinesthetic imagery can outperform visual imagery in systematic action imagery practice (Callow et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Combining visual and kinesthetic imagery can outperform visual imagery in systematic action imagery practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Callow et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: They show partly distinct brain activation patterns (Lee et al., 2019), while recruiting a core network shared across imagery modalities (Van Caenegem et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They show partly distinct brain activation patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Lee et al., 2019)</ref>, while recruiting a core network shared across imagery modalities <ref type="bibr">(Van Caenegem et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Below, we review research indicating that maintaining visual and kinesthetic information during action imagery can be linked to visuospatial and motor working memory: Visual imagery (not necessarily involving action) and visuospatial working memory, show similar neural patterns in the early visual cortex (Albers et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Below, we review research indicating that maintaining visual and kinesthetic information during action imagery can be linked to visuospatial and motor working memory: Visual imagery (not necessarily involving action) and visuospatial working memory, show similar neural patterns in the early visual cortex <ref type="bibr">(Albers et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitively, visual imagery likely relies on maintenance and manipulation processes associated with visuospatial working memory (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000; Gyselinck et al., 2007; Keogh & Pearson, 2011; Sherwood & Pearson, 2010; Valenti & Galera, 2020), being sensitive to standard working memory manipulations (selective interference, set size).

text.text: Visuospatial, but not verbal, interference reduces visual imagery vividness, whereas auditory imagery shows the opposite pattern (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000), and increasing set size (and thus working memory load) reduces imagery vividness, strength, and precision (Keogh & Pearson, 2017).

text.text: Recently executed motor acts are represented in the prefrontal and sensorimotor cortex (McDougle & Hillman, 2025), and individuals can maintain kinesthetic information of produced force (Vaillancourt & Russell, 2002) and reaching movements (Hillman et al., 2024; Jones & Henriques, 2010; Posner & Konick, 1966).
text.formatted: Recently executed motor acts are represented in the prefrontal and sensorimotor cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(McDougle & Hillman, 2025)</ref>, and individuals can maintain kinesthetic information of produced force <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Vaillancourt & Russell, 2002)</ref> and reaching movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Hillman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Jones & Henriques, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Posner & Konick, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Recall precision declines under standard working memory manipulations such as longer retention intervals (Adams & Dijkstra, 1966) and increasing set size (number of movements to remember; Hillman et al., 2024).

text.text: Rather than relying on language-based representations only, the temporary maintenance of action instructions draws on motor-related representations: Recall improves when the instructed actions (e.g., touch a circle; spin a cross) are enacted during encoding or recall (Allen & Waterman, 2015), and when they are imagined during encoding rather than verbally rehearsed (Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Rather than relying on language-based representations only, the temporary maintenance of action instructions draws on motor-related representations: Recall improves when the instructed actions (e.g., touch a circle; spin a cross) are enacted during encoding or recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Allen & Waterman, 2015)</ref>, and when they are imagined during encoding rather than verbally rehearsed <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These benefits of executing, anticipating or imagining instructed actions in maintaining and accurately recalling them are commonly interpreted as reflecting the formation of action plans that involve spatial-motoric coding (Allen & Waterman, 2015; Jaroslawska et al., 2016 Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;; Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These benefits of executing, anticipating or imagining instructed actions in maintaining and accurately recalling them are commonly interpreted as reflecting the formation of action plans that involve spatial-motoric coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Allen & Waterman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Jaroslawska et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, this evidence points to a contribution of visuospatial and motorrelated working memory during visual and kinesthetic action imagery.
Theoretical accounts differ in how motor coding is implemented within working memory.

It could be embedded within visuospatial working memory (Allen & Waterman, 2015; Li et al., 2022), or a separate motor component (Jaroslawska et al., 2016 (Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;; McDougle & Hillman, 2025; Smyth & Pendleton, 1989; Vannuscorps & Caramazza, 2016).
text.formatted: It could be embedded within visuospatial working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Allen & Waterman, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Li et al., 2022)</ref>, or a separate motor component <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Jaroslawska et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">McDougle & Hillman, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Smyth & Pendleton, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Vannuscorps & Caramazza, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The existence of a motor working memory that incorporates both afferent (e.g., visuospatial and somatosensory input) and efferent (e.g., motor commands) information has recently been proposed (McDougle & Hillman, 2025).
text.formatted: The existence of a motor working memory that incorporates both afferent (e.g., visuospatial and somatosensory input) and efferent (e.g., motor commands) information has recently been proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(McDougle & Hillman, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, motor working memory maintains and manipulates motor content retrospectively, temporarily maintaining recently executed movements so that movement features can be integrated for refinement, and prospectively, supporting motor plans that precede actions and guide future behavior.
Motor working memory can therefore serve as an internal buffer supporting imagery, manipulation, and rehearsal of future movements.

Such accounts delineate working memory processes in action imagery and can be integrated with theoretical accounts of action imagery, which have increasingly considered the role of working memory over recent decades.

Early proposals emphasized a functional similarity between imagined and executed actions, focusing on shared motor representations and neural substrates (Jeannerod, 2001), with little attention to the cognitive resources required to maintain imagery over time.
text.formatted: Early proposals emphasized a functional similarity between imagined and executed actions, focusing on shared motor representations and neural substrates <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Jeannerod, 2001)</ref>, with little attention to the cognitive resources required to maintain imagery over time.

text.text: Subsequent frameworks introduced predictive internal models that explain how simulated actions generate and evaluate anticipated sensory consequences (Grush, 2004; Rieger et al., 2024), highlighting the need to maintain and compare action-related information during imagery.
text.formatted: Subsequent frameworks introduced predictive internal models that explain how simulated actions generate and evaluate anticipated sensory consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Grush, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Rieger et al., 2024)</ref>, highlighting the need to maintain and compare action-related information during imagery.

text.text: The motor-cognitive model (Glover & Baran, 2017) makes this reliance on cognitive control explicit by proposing that imagery and execution overlap during the planning phase but diverge during realization.
text.formatted: The motor-cognitive model <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Glover & Baran, 2017)</ref> makes this reliance on cognitive control explicit by proposing that imagery and execution overlap during the planning phase but diverge during realization.

text.text: Whereas action execution benefits from automatic online sensorimotor control, action imagery depends more heavily on conscious elaboration to construct and monitor the simulated action.
Contemporary hybrid accounts of action imagery (for a discussion, see Hurst & Boe, 2022) propose a combined involvement of internal simulation and conscious monitoring.
text.formatted: Contemporary hybrid accounts of action imagery (for a discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Hurst & Boe, 2022)</ref> propose a combined involvement of internal simulation and conscious monitoring.

text.text: This aligns with the involvement of visuospatial and motor working memory processes.
In applied contexts, actions are systematically imagined to support motor rehabilitation (Dickstein & Deutsch, 2007; Kraeutner & Scott, 2025; López et al., 2019; McNeil et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In applied contexts, actions are systematically imagined to support motor rehabilitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Dickstein & Deutsch, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Kraeutner & Scott, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">López et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">McNeil et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such action imagery practice is often guided by verbal or written scripts (Holmes & Collins, 2001; Williams et al., 2013), which requires translating instructions accurately into mental action representations (Moran & O'Shea, 2020).
text.formatted: Such action imagery practice is often guided by verbal or written scripts <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Holmes & Collins, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Williams et al., 2013)</ref>, which requires translating instructions accurately into mental action representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Moran & O'Shea, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Final Position Judgement Tasks (FPJT) closely match related demands by requiring participants to imagine an unfolding action according to successive verbal (written or auditory) movement instructions and judge whether an image of a human figure matches the imagined final position (e.g., Donoff et al., 2018; Madan & Singhal, 2013; Schott, 2013).
text.formatted: Final Position Judgement Tasks (FPJT) closely match related demands by requiring participants to imagine an unfolding action according to successive verbal (written or auditory) movement instructions and judge whether an image of a human figure matches the imagined final position (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Donoff et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Madan & Singhal, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Schott, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Such behavioral tasks provide a means to examine cognitive processes underlying action imagery (Decety et al., 1989; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, McAteer, et al., 2025; Parsons, 1994).
text.formatted: Such behavioral tasks provide a means to examine cognitive processes underlying action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Decety et al., 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, McAteer, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Parsons, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Action-related language can automatically engage the motor system (Pulvermüller, 2005) and may draw on motor representations shared with action imagery (Dupont et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Action-related language can automatically engage the motor system <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Pulvermüller, 2005)</ref> and may draw on motor representations shared with action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Dupont et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When imagining verbally instructed movements, participants may therefore imagine visual and kinesthetic sensations associated with the unfolding action.
This may involve manipulating and maintaining visuospatial and motor-related representations in working memory.

Given the required comparison with a visual stimulus (position judgement image), during action imagery, participants may shift their inner gaze between their body parts to maintain their position as the action unfolds (visual rehearsal).
Yet, responses in action imagery ability tasks can rely on processes largely independent of action imagery (e.g., Burte et al., 2019; Mibu et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Yet, responses in action imagery ability tasks can rely on processes largely independent of action imagery (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Burte et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Mibu et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Lower sensorimotor expertise was shown to be associated with greater reliance on phonological representations rather than motor-related processing when remembering visually presented movement sequences (Moreau, 2013).
text.formatted: Lower sensorimotor expertise was shown to be associated with greater reliance on phonological representations rather than motor-related processing when remembering visually presented movement sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Moreau, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Further, the modality of mentally represented information likely depends on its input modality (Allen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Further, the modality of mentally represented information likely depends on its input modality <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Allen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, auditorily presented verbal instructions may be encoded phonologically and maintained through verbal rehearsal, demanding verbal working memory capacity.

These considerations suggest two non-mutually exclusive rehearsal strategies in the FPJT: visual rehearsal to maintain the imagined body position, and verbal rehearsal to maintain the verbal movement instructions.

Visual rehearsal is therefore conceptualized as an action imagery-related rehearsal strategy, whereas verbal rehearsal may either support action imagery or enable final position judgements without its' use.
Against this background, we examined the contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to final position judgements (see Table 1 for an overview of expectations).
text.formatted: Against this background, we examined the contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to final position judgements (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for an overview of expectations).

text.text: In the FPJT, participants listened to successive movement instructions and judged whether a subsequently presented image matched their imagined final position.

We introduced two working memory manipulations: articulatory suppression (repeating a syllable aloud throughout the task) was supposed to selectively disrupt verbal rehearsal, and varying set size (from three to six movements) to manipulate working memory load.

This allowed to examine how articulatory suppression affects maintaining verbally instructed action imagery, its associations with verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity and action imagery ability.

Because the FPJT requires processing auditory input, concurrently articulating a syllable could interfere with the initial phonological representation preceding the translation into visuospatial and motor-related representations (Yang et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Because the FPJT requires processing auditory input, concurrently articulating a syllable could interfere with the initial phonological representation preceding the translation into visuospatial and motor-related representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Yang et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore expected higher error rates and longer response times under articulatory suppression than at baseline.

Such impairment would indicate disrupted verbal rehearsal (Baddeley, 2012; Christoffels, 2006; Larsen & Baddeley, 2003), supporting action imagery maintenance or serving as an alternative rehearsal strategy.
text.formatted: Such impairment would indicate disrupted verbal rehearsal <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Baddeley, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Christoffels, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Larsen & Baddeley, 2003)</ref>, supporting action imagery maintenance or serving as an alternative rehearsal strategy.

text.text: Disrupted verbal rehearsal should be reflected in reported rehearsal strategy.
Nevertheless, if final position judgements did not rely primarily on verbal rehearsal, performance should remain above chance under articulatory suppression.
More movement instructions were expected to increase working memory load because participants had to maintain the action imagery longer and compare more details with the position judgement image.
We expected such set size-related effects to be reflected in higher error rates (Hillman et al., 2024) and longer response times (i.e., slower decision process; B. Pearson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: We expected such set size-related effects to be reflected in higher error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Hillman et al., 2024)</ref> and longer response times (i.e., slower decision process; B. <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Pearson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Further, we examined the unique associations of verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity with errors in final position judgements to disentangle their contributions to task performance.
Consistent with an action imagery process, we expected higher visuospatial working memory capacity to be associated with fewer errors in both conditions.
Verbal rehearsal could support action imagery maintenance at baseline but should be impaired under articulatory suppression.
We therefore expected higher verbal working memory capacity to be associated with fewer errors in the baseline condition only.

Additionally, we investigated whether the association between errors in final position judgements and visuospatial working memory capacity was stronger under articulatory suppression than in baseline.
Such a pattern would be consistent with greater reliance on action imagery-related processing when verbal rehearsal is disrupted.
Additionally, we expected to observe this shift in the reported frequencies of verbal and visual rehearsal.

Finally, as longer instruction sequences likely imposed higher working memory demands, we explored whether associations with verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity varied with the number of instructed movements.

We expected final position judgement performance to be positively associated with performance in other behavioral measures of action imagery ability, which engage processes of imagery manipulation (mental body rotation; Dahm et al., 2022) and maintenance (mental paper folding : Dahm & Draxler, 2022).

Final Position Judgement Task (FPJT).

The FPJT presents an adaptation of similar tasks (Madan & Singhal, 2013; Naito, 1994; Nishida et al., 1986; Schott, 2013) that addresses previous limitations and enables standardized administration (in-lab and online) and comparability across settings.

Mental Body Rotation Task.

To assess the association of the FPJT with a behavioral measure of mental rotation and perspective taking in action imagery (imagery manipulation), the Mental Body Rotation Task (Dahm et al., 2022; Steggemann et al., 2011) was administered.

Mental Paper Folding Task.

The Mental Paper Folding Task (Dahm & Draxler, 2022; Dahm & Sachse, 2025) was administered to assess the association of the FPJT with a behavioral measure targeting both imagery manipulation (spatial mental rotation) and imagery maintenance.
text.formatted: The Mental Paper Folding Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Dahm & Draxler, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Dahm & Sachse, 2025)</ref> was administered to assess the association of the FPJT with a behavioral measure targeting both imagery manipulation (spatial mental rotation) and imagery maintenance.

text.text: Participants imagined folding a two-dimensional paper grid into a threedimensional cube using their hands, focusing on internal visual and kinesthetic sensations, and judged as quickly and accurately as possible whether two colored sides overlap (Fig. 2B).
text.formatted: Participants imagined folding a two-dimensional paper grid into a threedimensional cube using their hands, focusing on internal visual and kinesthetic sensations, and judged as quickly and accurately as possible whether two colored sides overlap (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2B</ref>).

text.text: Stimulus complexity varied by number of folds (three to five) and direction changes (zero to four).
Participants responded with "x" (left index finger) for "no overlap" and "m" (right index finger) for "overlap".
The task included four easy practice trials with feedback and 24 trials in the test block (balanced fixed order; no feedback), with each trial starting with a onesecond fixation dot.
Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire 2 (VMIQ-2).

The German version (Dahm et al., 2019) of the VMIQ-2 (Roberts et al., 2008) served to familiarize participants with action imagery, thereby assessing their subjective vividness of third-person external visual (M±SD = 3.7±0.7; Cronbach's α = .89), first-person internal visual (M±SD = 3.9±0.7; Cronbach's α = .92), and kinesthetic action imagery (M±SD = 3.8±0.7; Cronbach's α = .90) in 12 everyday actions (five-point rating scale:1 = no image at all, I only know that I am thinking of the skill;5 = perfectly clear and vivid; values from first session).
text.formatted: The German version <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dahm et al., 2019)</ref> of the VMIQ-2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">(Roberts et al., 2008)</ref> served to familiarize participants with action imagery, thereby assessing their subjective vividness of third-person external visual (M±SD = 3.7±0.7; Cronbach's α = .89), first-person internal visual (M±SD = 3.9±0.7; Cronbach's α = .92), and kinesthetic action imagery (M±SD = 3.8±0.7; Cronbach's α = .90) in 12 everyday actions (five-point rating scale:1 = no image at all, I only know that I am thinking of the skill;5 = perfectly clear and vivid; values from first session).

text.text: Action imagery quality items.

To assess the subjective quality of participants' action imagery in the FPJT baseline (Cronbach's α = .82) and articulatory suppression condition (Cronbach's α = .84), and the relative involvement of sensory modalities, participants rated the ease and speed of imagery generation, imagery vividness, its maintenance and controllability, and the strength of visual imagery and imagined kinesthetic sensations on an eleven-point rating scale (0-10, with higher values indicating higher quality).
These action imagery quality items were adapted from the Sport Imagery Ability Measure (Watt, 2003).
text.formatted: These action imagery quality items were adapted from the Sport Imagery Ability Measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Watt, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Digit Span Task.
We applied the Digit Span Task to measure verbal working memory capacity.
In this task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of auditorily presented digits ranging from 1 to 9.
Digits were generated using Murf AI (https://murf.ai).
text.formatted: Digits were generated using Murf AI (<ref type="url" target="https://murf.ai">https://murf.ai</ref>).

text.text: Each trial involved a sequence of two to nine digits (presentation duration ~ 500ms/digit, inter-stimulus interval of 600ms).
Sequence length increased every two trials.
Immediately after the final digit and a 600ms interval, a signal tone of 250ms cued participants to recall the digits aloud in the order presented.
After a two-digit practice trial with feedback on whether the correct digits were recalled in the correct order, participants completed a test block consisting of 16 trials (no feedback).
Digit order was balanced across trials.
Performance was defined as the number of correctly recalled sequences (e.g., presenting 3-8-5-1 and recalling 3-9-5-1 was scored as incorrect).
Corsi Task.
We applied the Corsi Task (Corsi, 1972; Sdoia et al., 2019) to measure visuospatial working memory capacity.
text.formatted: We applied the Corsi Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Corsi, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Sdoia et al., 2019)</ref> to measure visuospatial working memory capacity.

text.text: In the Corsi Task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of illuminated squares.
In each trial, participants were presented with ten blue squares on a black background, with their locations varying across trials.
After an interval of 700ms, two to eight squares illuminated yellow for 700ms one after another.
Sequence length increase every two trials.

Immediately after the last square illuminated and a 350ms interval, a signal tone of 250ms cued participants to click the squares in the correct order, followed by feedback on whether the sequence was recalled correctly.
The task included a practice trial and 14 trials in the test block, with performance reflecting the number of correctly recalled sequences.
Participants attended two sessions of approximately 50 minutes, spaced 7 to 14 days apart (Fig. 3) to reduce practice effects and mental fatigue.
text.formatted: Participants attended two sessions of approximately 50 minutes, spaced 7 to 14 days apart (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>) to reduce practice effects and mental fatigue.

text.text: The order of the two sessions was counterbalanced across participants.
Each session began with the VMIQ-2, after which either the FPJT baseline or articulatory suppression condition was completed.
After the FPJT baseline condition, participants completed the Digit Span Task and the Mental Body Rotation Task.
After the FPJT articulatory suppression condition, they completed the Corsi Task and the Mental Paper Folding Task.

In both sessions, after completing the respective FPJT condition, participants indicated whether they had used (0 = no,1 = yes) visual rehearsal (mentally shifting gaze between instructed body parts to maintain imagery), and whether they had used verbal rehearsal (repeating instructions in inner speech).
Visual and verbal rehearsal were coded independently, such that participants could also report using both strategies.
Afterwards, they rated the task-specific action imagery quality items.
Note.
Participants completed either Session A or Session B first and completed the other session after an interval of 7-14 days.
The order of Sessions A and B was counterbalanced across participants.
VMIQ-2 = Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire 2.

We excluded one FPJT item (three movement instructions) with atypically high error rates (≥ 3 SD; baseline: 63.87%; articulatory suppression: 68.07%), as the upper body rotation likely obscured detection of the incorrectly directed arm movement, making its construct validity questionable.

Data from participants performing below chance were removed for the respective behavioral task (Mental Body Rotation Task: n = 1; Mental Paper Folding Task: n = 7), likely reflecting incorrect key allocation.
No univariate outliers (≥ 3 SD) were detected for the Digit Span Task or the Corsi Task.
Univariate outliers in trial-level response times were removed (Mental Body Rotation Task: 1.3%; Mental Paper Folding Task: 1.8%; FPJT baseline: 1.8%; FPJT articulatory suppression: 1.0%).
Response time analyses included trials with correct responses only, given that incorrect responses likely reflect different underlying processes (Ratcliff, 1978).

text.text: Except for the GLMMs described below, inferential analyses were based on participant-level aggregated scores.
Paired-samples t-tests were used to examine within-participant differences in continuous outcomes.
Above-chance performance under articulatory suppression was assessed by comparing participants' error rates against the chance level of 50% using a onetailed one-sample t-test.
Differences in the proportions of reported rehearsal strategies between conditions were examined using McNemar-tests.
All correlations were Pearson correlations and included available data of all participants.
Significance was set at p < .05.
text.formatted: Significance was set at p < .05.

text.text: Tests of differences in t-tests were one-tailed when corresponding to directional expectations and two-tailed otherwise.
Because response times were descriptively shorter under articulatory suppression, contrary to our directional expectation, we report results of an exploratory two-tailed t-test.
McNemar-tests, correlations, and GLMM coefficients were tested two-tailed.

To control alpha inflation due to multiple ttests and correlations, p-values were adjusted family-wise using Bonferroni-Holm correction (e.g., across all correlations between performance measures in the FPJT and action imagery ability tasks).

GLMMs (level 1: FPJT trial, level 2: participant) were fitted using maximumlikelihood estimation with a Laplace approximation and a binomial logit link to examine the unique contributions of verbal and visuospatial working memory capacities to final position judgment errors (0 = correct,1 = incorrect), accounting for number of movements and potential interactions with FPJT condition.
This multilevel approach was supported by a comparison of the intercept-only model with a random-intercept model, χ²(1) = 63.64, p < .001.
text.formatted: This multilevel approach was supported by a comparison of the intercept-only model with a random-intercept model, χ²(1) = 63.64, p < .001.

text.text: Non-binary predictors were grand-mean centered, and binary predictors were effectcoded.
Fixed and interaction effects were added stepwise based on theoretical expectations, with model selection guided by the Akaike information criterion (Akaike, 1974).
text.formatted: Fixed and interaction effects were added stepwise based on theoretical expectations, with model selection guided by the Akaike information criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Akaike, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: Odds ratios were unstandardized and obtained by exponentiating the unstandardized logit coefficients.
Random effects were approximately normal, no overdispersion was detected, and residuals showed no systematic patterns, indicating that binomial GLMM assumptions were met.

We specified in our expectations that if FPJT errors were primarily driven by verbal working memory, we should observe an association between lower odds of an FPJT error and participants' Digit Span in the baseline condition, but not under articulatory suppression.
A corresponding shift in strategy would further be supported if the association between lower FPJT error odds and Corsi Task performance was stronger under articulatory suppression than in baseline.
Neither interaction was significant, and neither Digit Span nor Corsi Task performance effects on errors interacted with the number of movements.

text.text: Reported visual rehearsal in the baseline condition was significantly positively correlated with kinesthetic imagery vividness in the VMIQ-2, whereas all other correlations were non-significant.
The present study examined the contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to maintaining verbally instructed action imagery.

Participants completed an adapted FPJT under baseline and articulatory suppression conditions, with articulatory suppression serving as a selective interference manipulation targeting verbal rehearsal.
In line with expectations, under articulatory suppression, error rates increased relative to baseline, while performance remained above chance.
Response times tended to increase with the number of instructed movements (i.e., set size effect), consistent with increasing working memory load.
Contrary to expectations, however, participants responded faster under articulatory suppression than in baseline, primarily for longer movement sequences.
Corsi Task performance, but not Digit Span Task performance, was associated with fewer final position judgement errors, partly consistent with our expectations.
While under articulatory suppression, reported use of verbal rehearsal was expectedly reduced, reported use of visual rehearsal did not increase.
Neither association differed significantly between FPJT conditions.
In line with expectations, FPJT performance was positively associated with performance in behavioral action imagery ability tasks.
In the baseline condition, reported visual rehearsal was associated with lower error rates.

The performance decline under articulatory suppression is consistent with the assumption of an initial phonological representation (Allen et al., 2023) and the loss of verbal rehearsal support in remembering movements (Xie et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The performance decline under articulatory suppression is consistent with the assumption of an initial phonological representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Allen et al., 2023)</ref> and the loss of verbal rehearsal support in remembering movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Xie et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Performance remained above chance under suppression, suggesting that final position judgements also involved processes beyond verbal rehearsal.

Further, although more than half of the participants reported verbal rehearsal at baseline, the overall pattern of findings indicates that it supported the maintenance of action imagery rather than drove performance.

First, strong correlations across baseline and articulatory suppression for both error rates and response times indicate substantial stability in individual performance and are consistent with shared processes contributing to both conditions.

Second, a high proportion of participants reported visually rehearsing body parts during imagery in both FPJT conditions, suggesting reliance on action imagery-related processes irrespective of selective interference with verbal rehearsal.

Third, visuospatial working memory capacity (approximated via Corsi Task performance), but not verbal working memory capacity (approximated via Digit Span Task performance), was related to fewer errors in final position judgments.

More specifically, individual differences in verbal working memory capacity did not account for additional variance in final position judgement errors, irrespective of articulatory suppression and the number of movements.

Although verbal working memory can support the retention of verbal instructions (Baddeley & Hitch, 2019; Yang et al., 2016), the present findings provide no evidence that its capacity meaningfully supported final position judgements.
text.formatted: Although verbal working memory can support the retention of verbal instructions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Baddeley & Hitch, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Yang et al., 2016)</ref>, the present findings provide no evidence that its capacity meaningfully supported final position judgements.

text.text: By contrast, higher visuospatial working memory capacity was associated with fewer errors across conditions, pointing to modality-specific processes rather than working memory capacity in general.

This interpretation aligns with evidence that visual imagery relies on maintenance and manipulation processes associated with visuospatial working memory (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000; Keogh & Pearson, 2011; Sherwood & Pearson, 2010; Valenti & Galera, 2020), which also support action imagery (Schott, 2013).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with evidence that visual imagery relies on maintenance and manipulation processes associated with visuospatial working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Baddeley & Andrade, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Keogh & Pearson, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Sherwood & Pearson, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Valenti & Galera, 2020)</ref>, which also support action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Schott, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Visual imagery thus likely contributed to maintaining action imagery generated from verbal instructions both at baseline and under articulatory suppression.

Converging neurophysiological evidence for action imagery involvement comes from an earlier FPJT, in which correct trials showed stronger mu suppression than incorrect trials, consistent with sensorimotor involvement in successful action imagery (Chen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Converging neurophysiological evidence for action imagery involvement comes from an earlier FPJT, in which correct trials showed stronger mu suppression than incorrect trials, consistent with sensorimotor involvement in successful action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Chen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, reported visual, but not verbal, rehearsal was associated with fewer errors at baseline.
This finding aligns with evidence that action imagery-related processing supports the maintenance of movement instructions more effectively than verbal rehearsal (Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This finding aligns with evidence that action imagery-related processing supports the maintenance of movement instructions more effectively than verbal rehearsal <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Further evidence for the involvement of action imagery in both conditions comes from the observed positive associations between performance in the FPJT and action imagery ability tasks.

Even when verbal rehearsal was not disrupted, final position judgments captured aspects of action imagery ability that overlap, but are not identical, to those assessed in mental body rotation and mental paper folding.

Unlike final position judgments, which require participants to generate action imagery from auditory input, manipulate and maintain it, and then compare it with an image, mental body rotation and mental paper folding elicit action imagery directly from visually presented stimuli.
Generating imagery "from scratch" in final position judgments likely places greater demands on imagery generation, maintenance, and inspection.

This may account for the small to moderate correlations, given similarly sized associations among behavioral tasks capturing different action imagery processes (Kraeutner et al., 2020; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, Van Caenegem, et al., 2025; Schott, 2013) and evidence that earlier FPJT versions did not correlate with a mental object rotation task that did not involve an actor (Madan & Singhal, 2013).
text.formatted: This may account for the small to moderate correlations, given similarly sized associations among behavioral tasks capturing different action imagery processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Kraeutner et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, Van Caenegem, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Schott, 2013)</ref> and evidence that earlier FPJT versions did not correlate with a mental object rotation task that did not involve an actor <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Madan & Singhal, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Because participants needed to translate verbal instructions into mental action representations, as in script-guided action imagery (Moran & O'Shea, 2020), articulatory suppression may also have impaired action imagery itself.
text.formatted: Because participants needed to translate verbal instructions into mental action representations, as in script-guided action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Moran & O'Shea, 2020)</ref>, articulatory suppression may also have impaired action imagery itself.

text.text: This is consistent with lower FPJTspecific action imagery quality ratings than at baseline and evidence that task-irrelevant auditory input can disrupt action imagery (Hohmann et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This is consistent with lower FPJTspecific action imagery quality ratings than at baseline and evidence that task-irrelevant auditory input can disrupt action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Hohmann et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, FPJT-specific action imagery quality ratings corresponded more consistently with accurate final position judgements under articulatory suppression.
This may reflect greater reliance on action imagery when verbal rehearsal was disrupted.
However, as errors were unrelated to verbal working memory capacity, the pattern might indicate greater awareness of imagery limitations under higher task demands.

Given the susceptibility of self-evaluations to self-enhancement (Alicke et al., 1995; Alicke & Sedikides, 2009), FPJT-specific ratings may reflect both subjective action imagery quality and experienced task difficulty.
text.formatted: Given the susceptibility of self-evaluations to self-enhancement <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alicke et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alicke & Sedikides, 2009)</ref>, FPJT-specific ratings may reflect both subjective action imagery quality and experienced task difficulty.

text.text: In both conditions, error rates and response times tended to increase with working memory load, manipulated via number of movements.
This set size effect is consistent with working memory involvement in maintaining action imagery (Baddeley, 2012; Cowan, 2001; Dunham et al., 2020; B. Pearson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This set size effect is consistent with working memory involvement in maintaining action imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Baddeley, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Cowan, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dunham et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">B. Pearson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with most participants reporting visual rehearsal of body parts in a serial manner, the response time pattern suggests a serial comparison process by imagined body part rather than a holistic visual inspection (Hegarty, 2004).
text.formatted: Consistent with most participants reporting visual rehearsal of body parts in a serial manner, the response time pattern suggests a serial comparison process by imagined body part rather than a holistic visual inspection <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Hegarty, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Participants likely performed a self-terminating serial comparison process, as identifying matching stimuli was slower than identifying non-matching stimuli.
In that case, detecting a non-matching position of a body part terminates the comparison of the presented image with one's imagery earlier than confirming a fully matching image.
One explanation for shorter response times under articulatory suppression, compared to the baseline, is an increase in task demands during the response phase due to the sustained repetition of "bla".

This, potentially effortful, articulatory suppression might have induced a shift toward prioritizing speed over accuracy, consistent with speed-accuracy trade-off mechanisms under increased cognitive load (Alister et al., 2024; Heitz, 2014).
text.formatted: This, potentially effortful, articulatory suppression might have induced a shift toward prioritizing speed over accuracy, consistent with speed-accuracy trade-off mechanisms under increased cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Alister et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Heitz, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because action imagery was more difficult to maintain under articulatory suppression, participants may have responded more quickly before it decayed further.
Additionally, articulatory suppression induced a rhythm to the task which may have contributed to faster responding.
Because the FPJT requires judging an image of a human figure, internal visual imagery was expected to be a core task demand (Krüger et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Because the FPJT requires judging an image of a human figure, internal visual imagery was expected to be a core task demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Krüger et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This motivated inclusion of the Corsi Task to test whether visuospatial maintenance accounts for unique variance in final position judgment errors beyond variance associated with maintaining verbal information (Digit Span Task).
Corsi Task performance was indeed associated with fewer errors, but the association was rather weak.
This may partly reflect the FPJT requirement to repeatedly update, rather than simply maintain, the imagined body position.
Future studies could therefore examine associations between performance in the FPJT and in tasks requiring working memory updating.
Beyond these manipulation demands, additional variance may arise from other maintenance processes not captured by our study.

Participants may have kinesthetically rehearsed the body position by repeatedly imagining movement-and posturerelated sensations (e.g., heaviness in a raised arm, stretch in the calf of a backward-extended leg, tension in the neck given the upwards lifted head).

Such a rehearsal strategy is plausible because the movement instructions likely engaged the motor system (Dupont et al., 2023), and participants were asked to use (and also reported) internal visual and kinesthetic action imagery.
text.formatted: Such a rehearsal strategy is plausible because the movement instructions likely engaged the motor system <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Dupont et al., 2023)</ref>, and participants were asked to use (and also reported) internal visual and kinesthetic action imagery.

text.text: Therefore, future studies could include a measure of motor working memory capacity to examine whether it explains variance in FPJT performance beyond visuospatial working memory capacity.

Although these considerations suggest that the FPJT involves action simulation, based on the behavioral data, the present study cannot rule out the possibility that participants solved the task using visual mental imagery detached from action imagery.
Selective interference paradigms comparing visuospatial and motor suppression could help determine the specific contribution of motor-related representations to FPJT performance.
Articulatory suppression inevitably involved mouth movements, which may have introduced motor interference.
This provides an additional account of impaired performance under articulatory suppression.
However, because these movements were task-irrelevant and relatively simple, substantial motor suppression effects appear unlikely.
In addition to selective interference paradigms, future studies could ask participants about a broader range of rehearsal strategies.
Yet, these self-reports are limited by their reliance on participants' conscious access to their strategy use.
Finally, the relative contribution of action imagery-related processes and verbal rehearsal likely depends on task demands (Chrysikou et al., 2014; Paivio, 1969).
text.formatted: Finally, the relative contribution of action imagery-related processes and verbal rehearsal likely depends on task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Chrysikou et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Paivio, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies could examine whether action imagery-related processes still contribute more than verbal rehearsal to maintaining action imagery when the presentation of movement instructions is self-paced.
Overall, our findings suggest that the FPJT engages action imagery and that imageryrelated visual rehearsal benefits task performance.

Together with the absence of an association between errors in final position judgements and verbal working memory capacity, the FPJT may be a suitable measure of aspects of action imagery ability that are relevant for action imagery practice guided by verbal instructions.

Earlier FPJT versions have already been used as behavioral measures of action imagery ability (e.g., Lambert et al., 2023 Lambert et al., , 2024 Lambert et al., , 2025;; Muraki & Pexman, 2021; Schott, 2012; Schott et al., 2021).

text.text: Ready-to-use OpenSesame and PsychoPy versions of the FPJT are available for local and online testing, with options to customize language, response mode (unimanual or bimanual), and feedback: https://github.com/carlacz/FPJT.
text.formatted: Ready-to-use OpenSesame and PsychoPy versions of the FPJT are available for local and online testing, with options to customize language, response mode (unimanual or bimanual), and feedback: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/carlacz/FPJT">https://github.com/carlacz/FPJT</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, our findings point to a greater contribution of action imagery-related processes than of verbal rehearsal to maintaining verbally instructed action imagery.

This interpretation is supported by above-chance performance under articulatory suppression and by the finding that visuospatial working memory capacity supported correct final position judgements, but verbal working memory capacity did not.
Visual rehearsal was widely reported in both conditions, suggesting reliance on action imagery-related processes already at baseline rather than a compensatory shift under articulatory suppression.

Given that visual rehearsal, but not verbal rehearsal, was associated with better FPJT performance, and that FPJT performance correlated with behavioral action imagery ability tasks, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.
